text: Anybody that works around the running shoe world would tell you that nothing is a end-all, be-all solution. The trend for the past few years are shoes are making their sockliners softer to improve step-in feel, which is how a lot of people make their purchases now. Hokas feel good when you try them on, and the average person assumes it will translate. Now it shifts back to maybe hitting those upper bounds for the entry-level runner, in a time where many more people are entry-level. That doesn't mean barefoot shoes are the solution. Everything in moderation, and excess requires balancing. Shoe rotations help mitigate these situations, but seeing someone's first running shoe as the Vomero Premium sparks a visceral reaction in me.

text: Yes. We aren't designed to have the senses in our feet completely blunted and dulled. Our soles have one of the highest densities of nerve endings on the body. The cushion leads to higher impact forces, a slower and less responsive gait, and longer ground contact time. All of these things spike injury risk exponentially. It's also my theory on why so many basketball players twist ankles and rip ligaments. They can't feel that their foot is in a bad position until they put 100% of their load on it. We've reduced and distorted the information signal that our feet naturally use to send to our brain feedback, so the control of our movement in an efficient and healthy way suffers.
